title: Two plugin eval suites are carried and nothing runs them
description:
This repository carries two Claude Code plugin eval suites for the opum-quest plugin and nothing runs them. `claude plugin eval` went generally available on 2026-09-11 in Claude Code 2.1.269 (documented at https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugin-evals), which makes wiring them possible; whether to do it is a cost decision, and there is a trap in the CI shape that has to be answered before they could ever gate anything.

MEASURED HERE, 2026-09-11:
  evals/quest-task-request/  prompt.md + graders/{outcome.md,skill-fired.md}
  evals/quest-no-trigger/    prompt.md + graders/
  evals/results/             two run directories, both 2026-09-05
  No runner script in scripts/, no eval script in package.json, and nothing
  in .github/workflows references evals at all.
  Local Claude Code is 2.1.269, so the GA command is available on this machine.

So the suites exist, were last exercised by hand six days ago, and are not wired to anything. That is the same class this session spent the day on, from a third angle: a check nobody runs proves nothing, and a green dated 2026-09-05 is a timestamp rather than a standing fact. The suites are currently the second kind of artifact -- carried, plausible-looking, and silent.

THE TRAP, which is why this is not a straightforward wiring job. Per the documented CI shape, a run that hits a plan usage limit SCORES 0 WITHOUT THE SUITE BEING MARKED PARTIAL. So a red can mean the skill regressed, or it can mean the account ran out of budget, and the two are indistinguishable from the result. Wiring that into a required check would manufacture exactly the failure this repository documented today in tracker-integrity.yml, inverted: instead of an absent signal that looks like a pass, an infrastructure condition that looks like a regression. A gate whose red does not distinguish "the thing broke" from "the runner ran out of money" trains people to ignore it, which is worse than not having it.

COST. `claude plugin eval` consumes model usage per run and the documented shape takes --max-cost-usd, pinned --model and --judge-model. Running two suites on every PR has a real recurring bill attached, which makes the cadence a decision for the repository's user rather than something to infer -- and the cadence interacts with the trap, because the more often it runs the more likely a usage-limit red becomes.

OPTIONS TO DECIDE BETWEEN, not decided here:
A. Leave as-is. Suites stay documentation of intent. Costs nothing, proves nothing.
B. Add a runner script and an explicit manual/dispatch-only workflow, pinned model and judge-model, --json to a results path, --max-cost-usd set. Run deliberately before a plugin change ships rather than on every PR. No gating, so the trap cannot mislead a required check; the human reading the result can tell a budget red from a real one by looking.
C. As B, plus a scheduled run at a cadence low enough to keep the bill predictable.
D. As B, plus gating -- only if the usage-limit case can first be made distinguishable from a genuine failure. On today's documented behaviour it cannot be, so this option is blocked on an upstream change rather than on effort here.

This session's read, offered rather than taken: B is the honest shape now, and D is the one worth wanting but is not available yet. The distinguishing question for any future revisit is narrow and checkable -- can a usage-limited run be told apart from a scored failure in the JSON output? If that becomes yes, D opens.

Raised by the orchestrator as a fact with no action requested. Filed so the finding is not lost, deliberately left To Do.

acceptanceCriteria.text: A decision exists between the recorded options, with its cost cadence stated, since running the suites bills real usage
If the suites are wired, a red result distinguishes a genuine failure from a usage-limited run, or the wiring is explicitly non-gating and says why
The eval results in evals/results carry the date and the CLI version they were produced with, so a green is never read as a standing fact

implementationNotes:
CORRECTION, 2026-09-11, and the error is mine. This task recorded that the usage-limit case cannot be distinguished from a genuine failure 'on today's documented behaviour'. That is FALSE, and it was false when I wrote it. I asserted a fact about documented behaviour from a one-line summary without reading the documentation.

The page says the opposite, verbatim: 'If your account reaches its plan's usage limit or an API rate limit while a suite is running, each later run ends with that error, is graded on what it produced, and usually scores 0. The suite still finishes and isn't marked partial, so the result can look like a regression. Check the NOTES column or cases[].arms.with[].error in the JSON for the limit message before trusting the scores, then re-run after the limit resets, with --runs 1 or a --case filter if you need to stay under it.'

So the suite-level partial flag genuinely is not set -- that half was right -- but the limit message IS carried per run, one level below where I looked. Verified two ways rather than taken: I read the documentation page directly, and I read opum-fleet's scripts/run-eval.sh, which iterates Object.values(c.arms), reads run.error, counts errored runs and prints the first message back, with a comment stating the same behaviour. Also learned in the same read: --max-cost-usd is a DIFFERENT case and does mark partial: true with reason cost_ceiling and exit 2. I had been conflating the two.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE OPTIONS: option D is no longer blocked. A gate can tell a budget red from a regression by reading cases[].arms.with[].error rather than the aggregate. The shape lore-cli chose -- scheduled, non-blocking, --max-cost-usd, both --model and --judge-model pinned -- is available now. What remains is the cost decision, which stays with this repository's user; the technical blocker I recorded does not exist.

The irony is exact and worth leaving in the record rather than tidying: I wrote that the distinguishing question was 'narrow and checkable' and then did not check it. Same class as the four defects this session already logged, committed in the act of describing them.
